title: Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation
learning_outcomes: Explain how headers, media types, and content negotiation affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from general, request, and response headers to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on headers, media types, and content negotiation in web networking and http fundamentals. You will connect general, request, and response headers to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying general, request, and response headers deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.caption: Follow the 5 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: HTTP is the application-layer request/response protocol; message semantics live in methods, status codes, and headers. In this lesson, treat “Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation
content_blocks.code:
GET /v1/tasks?limit=20 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.test
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store

{"items": [], "limit": 20}
content_blocks.expected_output: The example shows a request target and headers followed by a response status, metadata, and JSON representation. example.test is illustrative and is not a live service.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “General, request, and response headers”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Content-Type and Accept” and “Unsupported media types and representations”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Inspect the complete request and response before diagnosing an API failure. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating headers, media types, and content negotiation. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “General, request, and response headers” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating headers, media types, and content negotiation as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: HTTP is the application-layer request/response protocol; message semantics live in methods, status codes, and headers. In this lesson, treat “Headers, Media Types, and Content Negotiation” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 17: Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests.
